segments.narration: A pig ate a man's potatoes and nearly started a war. San Juan Island, June 1859. One shot, one dead pig, two empires.
The farmer was American. The pig worked for the Hudson's Bay Company. Both countries claimed the island, and neither government would back down an inch.
Two months later: four hundred sixty-one American soldiers and fourteen cannons against five Royal Navy warships, seventy guns, two thousand one hundred and forty men.
All of it over a pig. The British admiral flatly refused to fire, saying he would not go to war over a squabble about a pig.
So they shared the island instead, for thirteen years, until an arbitration ruling handed it to America in 1872. Total casualties: the pig.

verdicts.claim: On 15 June 1859 an American settler, Lyman Cutlar, shot a pig that was eating his potatoes on San Juan Island.

verdicts.claim: By 10 August 1859 Colonel Silas Casey commanded 461 American soldiers with 14 cannons, opposed by five Royal Navy warships carrying 70 guns and 2,140 men.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives exactly these figures for 10 August 1859, under Colonel Silas Casey and Captain Geoffrey Hornby.

verdicts.claim: Rear Admiral Robert L. Baynes refused to escalate, describing the dispute as a squabble about a pig.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia records that Baynes arrived, refused to escalate, and called it a matter 'over a squabble about a pig'.

verdicts.claim: The two sides held a joint military occupation until arbitration under the 1871 Treaty of Washington ruled for the United States on 21 October 1872, and the pig was the only casualty.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia records joint military occupation from 1859, the 1871 Treaty of Washington arbitration, the Geneva commission's ruling for the United States on 21 October 1872, and the pig as the only casualty. Thirteen years spans 1859 to the British withdrawal in November 1872.
